   • A wave of setbacks has left President Trump frustrated and telling aides he doesn’t have enough political allies defending him on television.

   • A shortage of oil tankers is threatening to keep gas prices high .

   • The Trump administration is preparing to impose sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court.

   • Few investors are feeling more pain from rising interest rates than America’s apartment landlords.

READ IT HERE FIRST   The IRS is cracking down on a favorite way the ultrarich pass on money.   Wealthy Americans have for years used a popular type of trust to transfer fortunes to their children without paying hefty gift and estate taxes. Now they’re on high alert . The Internal Revenue Service is calling foul on an heiress who used the strategy—and is slapping her and her husband with a $736 million tax bill. Chuck and Trisha Elcan of Nashville, Tenn., are fighting back in U.S. Tax Court, disputing the agency’s claim that they made missteps with grantor-retained annuity trusts, or GRATs, which they used to shift money to their three daughters. The Elcan case offers a look inside the complex strategies the ultrarich deploy to build intergenerational wealth and how those tactics can sometimes test the boundaries of tax rules, reports Ashlea Ebeling.

   5.   Meet the Miami residents plotting Cuba’s future.   As Cuba sinks deeper into crisis, wealthy exiles are racing to plot its future from Miami, where the Trump administration is turning for ideas, political support and private capital to rebuild the country if the regime falls. Across the city, they are gaming out who could lead Cuba’s nine million people. The effort has drawn billionaires and Trump-linked power-brokers, the scions of Cuban-American dynasties built on sugar, and immigrants who amassed fortunes over decades in the U.S. Some have a direct line to the Trump administration, report José de Córdoba and Vera Bergengruen. The feverish preparations have been fueled by three words Trump has repeated since the capture of Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro in January: “Cuba is next.”

SEE THE STORY   Detroiters see an economy that isn’t working for them and want change ahead of November’s election.     Photo: Annie Zhao   WSJ’s Joshua Jamerson: Growing up in the city that put Americans on wheels taught me a lot about hard work and opportunity. But perhaps above all, I learned that the two are often inseparable. So ahead of the midterm elections, I wanted to go back home to find out whether the Trump economy is making it easier or harder for working people to get ahead. Overwhelmingly, the dozen or so Detroiters I spoke with said the cost of living was getting out of control. But what surprised me wasn’t the economic pessimism itself—it was how specific the frustration had become, and who people blamed.

       7. HAPPENING TODAY   • Trump is expected to meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. He is also set to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron, a day before Trump’s scheduled remarks to the U.N. General Assembly.

   • 📰 Today’s paper

As an iconic American brand, the motorcycle maker frequently finds itself targeted when foreign governments hit back against U.S. trade policies—most recently facing a 50% import duty imposed by Canada. While Harley has eaten trade costs in the past to protect its customer base, the company has declined to outline its plans for Canada .

       9. AND FINALLY…   Gym bros are going to Pilates—and shaking like a Chihuahua as they leave.   Boyfriends and husbands are learning the hard way that their female companions are not going to 7 a.m. classes just to stretch. Gym bros accustomed to bench-presses and burpees swagger into serene studios expecting to spend 50 minutes doing light exercises with toy dumbbells. Many severely underestimate the difficulty of Pilates or its high-intensity offshoots, which are built on low-impact movements that give priority to core strength, posture and slow burn. They leave broken men—much to their partners’ delight.

1. FROM MY DESK

 

With six weeks until the midterms, the battle for control of Congress—and the direction of both parties—is entering its final, decisive stretch. At the Journal, our focus this election is to help you understand the people, places and ideas shaping the country.

 

We’re taking you beyond Washington and into the places where politics is lived. Through our Rooted In series, our reporters return to their hometowns to deliver on-the-ground perspective. This morning, Joshua Jamerson checks in from Detroit to see how working-class voters are feeling ahead of crucial Michigan races.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

The IRS is cracking down on a favorite way the ultrarich pass on money.

 

Wealthy Americans have for years used a popular type of trust to transfer fortunes to their children without paying hefty gift and estate taxes. Now they’re on high alert. The Internal Revenue Service is calling foul on an heiress who used the strategy—and is slapping her and her husband with a $736 million tax bill. Chuck and Trisha Elcan of Nashville, Tenn., are fighting back in U.S. Tax Court, disputing the agency’s claim that they made missteps with grantor-retained annuity trusts, or GRATs, which they used to shift money to their three daughters. The Elcan case offers a look inside the complex strategies the ultrarich deploy to build intergenerational wealth and how those tactics can sometimes test the boundaries of tax rules, reports Ashlea Ebeling.

 

5.

 

Meet the Miami residents plotting Cuba’s future.

 

As Cuba sinks deeper into crisis, wealthy exiles are racing to plot its future from Miami, where the Trump administration is turning for ideas, political support and private capital to rebuild the country if the regime falls. Across the city, they are gaming out who could lead Cuba’s nine million people. The effort has drawn billionaires and Trump-linked power-brokers, the scions of Cuban-American dynasties built on sugar, and immigrants who amassed fortunes over decades in the U.S. Some have a direct line to the Trump administration, report José de Córdoba and Vera Bergengruen. The feverish preparations have been fueled by three words Trump has repeated since the capture of Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro in January: “Cuba is next.”

CONTENT FROM: KEARNEY
 
 
Impact First: A Radically Different Future Within Reach
 
Meaningful impact demands radically different thinking. Yet our research shows leaders are boxed in: 66% say incentives reward quick wins over lasting impact, and 72% say uncertainty is forcing a more reactive stance. The tension is real—between the impact leaders want and the systems holding them back. How do you close the gap?

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Detroiters see an economy that isn’t working for them and want change ahead of November’s election.

 
 
Photo: Annie Zhao
 

WSJ’s Joshua Jamerson: Growing up in the city that put Americans on wheels taught me a lot about hard work and opportunity. But perhaps above all, I learned that the two are often inseparable. So ahead of the midterm elections, I wanted to go back home to find out whether the Trump economy is making it easier or harder for working people to get ahead. Overwhelmingly, the dozen or so Detroiters I spoke with said the cost of living was getting out of control. But what surprised me wasn’t the economic pessimism itself—it was how specific the frustration had become, and who people blamed.

That’s the cost to Harley-Davidson of swallowing retaliatory tariffs in the past eight years to keep retail prices stable. As an iconic American brand, the motorcycle maker frequently finds itself targeted when foreign governments hit back against U.S. trade policies—most recently facing a 50% import duty imposed by Canada. While Harley has eaten trade costs in the past to protect its customer base, the company has declined to outline its plans for Canada.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Gym bros are going to Pilates—and shaking like a Chihuahua as they leave.

 

Boyfriends and husbands are learning the hard way that their female companions are not going to 7 a.m. classes just to stretch. Gym bros accustomed to bench-presses and burpees swagger into serene studios expecting to spend 50 minutes doing light exercises with toy dumbbells. Many severely underestimate the difficulty of Pilates or its high-intensity offshoots, which are built on low-impact movements that give priority to core strength, posture and slow burn. They leave broken men—much to their partners’ delight.
